title: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed

fields.label: Label
fields.value: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: It is a general law of nature that no organism fertilises itself for an unlimited number of generations; an occasional cross with another individual, perhaps at long intervals, is indispensable, even in hermaphrodites.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it is a general law of nature (utterly ignorant though we be of the meaning of the law) that no organic being self-fertilises itself for an eternity of generations; but that a cross with another individual is occasionally—perhaps at very long intervals—indispensable.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species”. Scope: all plants and animals, especially hermaphrodites

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The universal assertion is falsifiable by persistent obligate-selfing lineages and genomic methods can detect rare crosses. Existing data cover many plants and some animals, but cannot establish an eternal necessity across all organisms.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify lineages with genomic evidence of prolonged obligate selfing and test persistence, fertility and genetic load through time. Any indefinitely selfing, persistent lineage would refute the universal claim, while recurrent outcrossing across well-sampled nominal selfers would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
An unlimited number of generations cannot be observed.

Rare outcrossing is difficult to exclude from finite genomic samples.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Prolonged selfing or asexuality leaves genomic signatures, and the decisive lineages plus a sexual-system database are public. A universal claim can be challenged by those lineages without sequencing every hermaphrodite, but the flagship cases remain ambiguous because cryptic sex is hard to exclude. The analysis is standard for a small team and still short of a clean confirmation or refutation across plants and animals.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For hermaphrodites and candidate ancient asexuals, test genomes for meiosis genes, allele divergence, and the age of asexuality. The claim would be confirmed if every well-sampled lineage shows occasional outcrossing or a recent loss of sex. It would be refuted by a lineage that has persisted for many millions of years with no sex and no genomic sign of decline that an occasional cross would be needed to prevent.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many hermaphrodites still lack genomes dense enough for a Meselson-effect test.

Rare sex, gene conversion, and horizontal transfer can mimic or mask long-term asexuality.

Indispensable is a fitness claim that extant genomes record only indirectly.
